messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: ODE matters
parts:
Dear all,

with the cvodes implementation I introduced what I called the ode_model class. This class binds together what I think belongs together in this context. The class will allow us to cut down existing code, make the ODE code more readable and it will also easily enable the use of analytic Jacobians with ODEs at some point (such that AD is avoided). Please find attached a PDF which lays out my thinking.

Comments are very welcome. Throughout the current cvodes pull request it was moreover suggested to rename the ode_model class into ode only. My motivation to call this class more than just ode is that the class encapsulates more than only the ODE RHS, but all additional stuff like Jacobians. So proposals for names are

- ode_model
- ode
- ode_system
- other???

Any input on this would be great. Thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

I don’t think template specialization is useful here as there’s no
inputs that can be used to choose between implementations, no?
Just use an object oriented pattern with a base_ode_system that
does autodiff and we can add a specialization that overrides the
default behavior later. The specific ode_system implementation
would then be templated in the integrate_ode functions.

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ODE matters
parts:
ode_system is a great name, I will adjust.

Let me explain in more detail, how this is supposed to work. So the ode_system has a declaration like

template<typename F>
ode_system {
ode_system(F model, std::vector<double> theta, ...other stuff to call RHS...)

void operator()(t, y, dy_dt) => calls the functor F to get the ODE RHS

void jacobian_S(t,y,dy_dt,Jy) => calculates the Jacobian wrt to states

void jacobian_SP(t,y,dy_dt,Jy,Jtheta) => calculates the Jacobian wrt to states and parameters

};

So the ode_system is templated by the ODE RHS functor F. Our ODE integrators then use an instance of ode_system<ODE_to_be_solved> in their code. The generic implementation would use auto-diff to get the Jacobians. In case we want to specify analytic Jacobians, then all what would need to be done is define some where a

ode_system<hard_stiff_ODE> {

... definition of ODE RHS ...
... analytic definitions of Jacobian functions ...

};

And then the integrators would use fully analytic Jacobians instead of auto-diff.

An implementation can be found here (I still need to rename):

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-262-CVODES-2/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/ode_model.hpp

I have tried this approach and it works nicely. For systems where it makes sense to provide the analytic Jacobians, you get 2-3x speedup. Moreover, there are code-generation toolboxes out there which start off with SBML (XML language to describe ODEs) and give you code-generated C++ sources with analytic Jacobians.

I hope that makes sense.

Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ODE matters
parts:
> On Apr 26, 2016, at 3:19 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ode_system is a great name, I will adjust.
>
> Let me explain in more detail, how this is supposed to work. So the ode_system has a declaration like
>
> template<typename F>
> ode_system {
> ode_system(F model, std::vector<double> theta, ...other stuff to call RHS...)
>
> void operator()(t, y, dy_dt) => calls the functor F to get the ODE RHS

F is a template parameter --- model is the functor if F refers to a class
that implements operator().
> void jacobian_S(t,y,dy_dt,Jy) => calculates the Jacobian wrt to states

No caps in identifiers if at all possible and I'd also rather avoid
uncommon one-letter abbreviations.
> void jacobian_SP(t,y,dy_dt,Jy,Jtheta) => calculates the Jacobian wrt to states and parameters

You can just call these both "jacobian" if you want as they're distinguished
by arguments. Otherwise, "jacobian_state" and "jacobian_state_param" or something
more descriptive.

> };

What's the concept for F? That is, what is required of F to be
valid in this setting?
> So the ode_system is templated by the ODE RHS functor F.

F is a class type, not a functor. Sorry to be so picky on terminology,
but these discussions are a lot easier for me to understand if we get
the naming right.

> Our ODE integrators then use an instance of ode_system<ODE_to_be_solved> in their code. The generic implementation would use auto-diff to get the Jacobians. In case we want to specify analytic Jacobians, then all what would need to be done is define some where a
>
> ode_system<hard_stiff_ODE> {
>
> ... definition of ODE RHS ...
> ... analytic definitions of Jacobian functions ...
>
> };
>
> And then the integrators would use fully analytic Jacobians instead of auto-diff.

Sounds good.

The altenrative would be to have ode_system be a base class; that
can be less efficient than what you're doing but also clearer. So
you'll have to use your judgment.

> An implementation can be found here (I still need to rename):
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-262-CVODES-2/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/ode_model.hpp

The raw streams are probably going to have to be writers. I frown
upon pointers. I'd also much rather see references than pointers in
things like:

std::ostream* msgs_;

As soon as you have pointers, there's a possiblity that they're 0 and
thus a possibility of a runtime error from non-instantiation. And it
makes the syntax uglier (-> rather than .).

> I have tried this approach and it works nicely. For systems where it makes sense to provide the analytic Jacobians, you get 2-3x speedup. Moreover, there are code-generation toolboxes out there which start off with SBML (XML language to describe ODEs) and give you code-generated C++ sources with analytic Jacobians.
Cool.
> I hope that makes sense.

Yup. Thanks for clarifying.

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ODE matters
parts:
Many thanks Bob for your comments!

I will then use a single jacobian function and the specific version to be used will be identified by the function signature.

As this will be a new object within the Stan math system - what tests would be needed? I am asking as to what principles to apply here as this is not 100% clear to me what exactly the rationale is, i.e. I would simply call the public functions in tests as they are intended to be used and check results. So the jacobian function can be easily tested with the jacobian function from math.

Sebastian

PS: The speed gain really makes a difference - in particular for those nasty michaelis-menten ODE systems which are used frequently in PK.
